title: What the PMP Costs, and Which Costs PMI Doesn't Set
dek: PMI charges $405 for members and $655 for non-members, and that is the part of the bill you can look up. The costs that actually decide your budget — the required training, the renewal you pay every three years, and the time — are set by other people or not published at all.

seo.metaTitle: What the PMP Costs (And Which Costs PMI Doesn't Set)
seo.metaDescription: PMI charges $405 for members, $655 otherwise. The costs that decide your budget — training, renewal, PDU time — aren't set by PMI at all.

sources.label: PMI — How to maintain your certification
PMI — Continuing Certification Requirements (CCR) Handbook, 2026 edition

body.richText: The exam fee is the number everyone looks up, and it is the one line on the bill that PMI actually sets. The education PMI requires is sold by other companies, at prices PMI does not publish. The renewal due every three years depends on your membership status and on where you are. And the biggest commitment the credential asks of you is not money at all. What follows is an attempt at the whole shape, with the figures we could confirm kept apart from the ones we could not.

body.text: What PMI charges, and what it doesn't

body.richText: PMI's exam fee is $405 for members and $655 for non-members. Membership itself is $139 a year and is a separate product from the certification — you can sit the exam without it. Those are the figures that come straight from the certifying body, and they are the reliable part of the budget. Treat them as the starting point rather than the final word: PMI serves pricing through your account, so what appears at checkout can depend on where you are. Confirm your own figure before you pay.

richText: PMI requires qualifying education, but it does not publish a single price for the required 35 hours. Most applicants need 35 contact hours of project management education before they can apply; if you already hold an active CAPM, that requirement is covered, which is worth checking before you buy anything. Providers set their own prices, so there is no single "PMP training cost" issued by PMI — anyone quoting you one is quoting a seller, or an average of sellers. We have deliberately not published a range here, because every source we found for one was itself selling training. The current rules are in our

rows: The exam fee, and 35 contact hours of education
PMI sets the exam fee; training providers set the education
A further exam fee if you don't pass first time
Membership, prep courses, question banks, books, PDU bundles
Renewal every three years, and 60 PDUs each cycle
PMI sets the requirement; what you spend meeting it is largely your choice

body.richText: Only part of one line in that table is both required and priced by the organization issuing the credential. Everything else is sold by someone else, triggered by an outcome, or chosen by you — which is why two people can both "get the PMP" and spend amounts that are not comparable. On the conditional row we are being deliberately unhelpful: a further attempt costs a further fee, but we have not confirmed the current amount or the retake rules at source, so we are not quoting a number we would only be repeating from somewhere else.

body.text: Membership is a $111 question at exam time

body.richText: PMI membership is optional, costs $139 a year, and lowers the exam fee. That makes the decision arithmetic rather than a matter of loyalty, and the arithmetic is short enough to check.

CertNorth calculation. Non-member route: $655 for the exam. Member route: $139 for membership plus $405 for the exam, which is $544. Joining is $111 cheaper for a single first attempt, and you also hold a year's membership at the end of it. Assumptions: PMI's current published fees, one exam attempt, no regional variation, and any one-time application fee excluded because we could not confirm its amount. The direction of this result holds for as long as membership costs less than the $250 gap between the two exam fees.

richText: That is the exam-only break-even, and it is the narrow question. Whether membership is worth keeping afterwards is a different calculation with a different answer, because the renewal discount is much smaller than the exam discount and recurs against an annual fee — we work that through separately in

. Two things the calculation above deliberately does not do: it puts no value on the library, the webinars or the chapter access, because that depends entirely on whether you use them, and it does not assume you will renew membership at all.

body.text: Sixty PDUs, and why eight is the number that matters

body.richText: Keeping the PMP requires 60 professional development units in every three-year cycle, and the composition matters more than the total. The requirement is a set of limits nested inside each other, which is where most summaries of it go wrong.

body.caption: How a PMP renewal cycle is constrained (source: PMI, Continuing Certification Requirements Handbook). Education carries a minimum; the others are maximums.
rows: Learning activities — the only category with a floor rather than a ceiling
Contributing rather than consuming: mentoring, volunteering, writing, speaking, and working in the role
One activity inside Giving Back — the credit for doing the job itself

richText: The last two rows are the ones that get conflated, and conflating them produces a comfortable but wrong conclusion. Working in your certified role is one activity within Giving Back, not the whole category — so simply holding a project management job contributes at most 8 of the 60 PDUs you need, and nothing at all toward the 35 that must be Education. The rest of Giving Back can carry more, but it takes deliberate contribution: mentoring someone, volunteering, writing, speaking. The consequence for your calendar is real: at least 35 Education PDUs is a floor, and no job clears it on its own. One coincidence worth naming before it confuses you, because it confuses almost everyone: the 35 contact hours you need before sitting the exam and the 35 Education PDUs you need in each renewal cycle are separate requirements at different stages — one is a condition of applying, the other a condition of keeping the credential afterwards. Which activities fall into which category, and the limits on each, are in

link.text: our guide to how PDUs actually work

body.text: Money and time are separate budgets

body.richText: It is tempting to convert hours into money and produce a single number. We are not going to, because it would require inventing an hourly rate for you, and the result would say more about the rate we picked than about the PMP. The two budgets are better kept apart, because they are constrained differently — you can borrow money for a course, and you cannot borrow the evenings. The time side looks like this:

items: Qualifying: 36 or 60 months of documented project experience, depending on whether you hold a four-year degree. By far the longest item, and no amount of spending shortens it
Education: 35 contact hours before you can apply
Preparation: variable, and it depends mostly on how recent and how broad your project experience is
Maintenance: 60 PDUs every three years, at least 35 of them Education — roughly 20 hours a year, for as long as you hold the credential

body.text: Why we won't give you a ten-year total

richText: A ten-year cost of ownership would be the natural way to finish this, and plenty of sites publish one. We are not going to, for three reasons worth stating rather than hiding. First, the renewal fee is not a single universal number — it depends on your membership status when you renew and, like the exam fee, on how PMI prices for your location, so multiplying one figure by three cycles would manufacture precision we do not have. Second, the education requirement is priced by companies we would be guessing about. Third, any long-run total that weights a retake by the chance of failing needs a pass rate, and PMI has not published one for around two decades — the numbers in circulation come from training providers' own students or from a passing score retired years ago, which we set out in

link.text: our piece on the PMP pass rate

richText: . What we can give you is the shape: one exam fee, one education requirement, then a renewal event every three years for as long as you keep the credential. Price those three against your own PMI account and you will have a better ten-year figure than any we could responsibly publish.

body.text: What changes at the end of 2026

richText: One scheduled rule change affects the required education, which makes it a budgeting question rather than a study one. As things stand, the 35 contact hours may come from any eligible provider, in any format. Late in 2026 that narrows: PMI has announced restrictions on which providers may deliver taught, instructor-led hours for application purposes. Nothing has changed yet, and self-paced study currently still counts. The practical implication is about timing rather than rules — if you are budgeting for taught training you will sit around or after that point, confirm the provider qualifies before you pay, because the cheapest option available today may not be one that counts by then. The exact wording and the full current requirements are in

items: Sign in to PMI and read the exam fee shown for your own account. That is the price you will be charged, and it is the only one that matters
Decide on membership before you book, not after — the discount applies to a fee you have not yet paid
Check whether an active CAPM already covers your 35 contact hours before buying any training
Get a written quote for the education you actually need, from a provider whose status you have confirmed
Add one renewal cycle to whatever you calculate, so the number you carry in your head is the cost of holding the credential rather than of passing the exam
